L75/3.about: Debussy’s most famous piano piece, its title meaning ’Moonlight’, taken from a poem by Paul Verlaine. A hazy, floating melody drifts over rich, impressionistic harmony, evoking stillness and light rather than telling any literal story — emblematic of Debussy’s break from the more narrative or dramatic programme music of the nineteenth century.
L75/3.ctx: Composed around 1890 and substantially revised before its publication in 1905 as the third piece of the Suite bergamasque, itself named after a phrase from Verlaine’s poetry evoking masked figures at a moonlit, melancholy revel.
facts: Debussy’s single most famous piano piece.
Takes its title from a poem by Paul Verlaine.
The third piece of the Suite bergamasque.

L117/8.about: Titled ’The Girl with the Flaxen Hair’, one of Debussy’s most tender and immediately accessible works, its gentle melody inspired by a poem of the same name by Leconte de Lisle depicting a young woman in a summer meadow.
L117/8.ctx: Composed in 1909–10 as the eighth of the twelve préludes of Book 1, part of Debussy’s mature practice of giving each prelude an evocative title, printed unusually at the end rather than the beginning of the score, so as not to constrain the performer’s imagination in advance.
facts: Its title comes from a poem by Leconte de Lisle.
One of the most frequently performed and recorded of all Debussy’s piano works.
Debussy printed the evocative titles of his préludes at the end of each piece, not the beginning.

L117/10.about: Titled ’The Sunken Cathedral’, inspired by a Breton legend of a cathedral that rises from the sea at dawn, its bells and chant audible before it sinks once more beneath the waves. Built on massive, bell-like parallel chords and a slowly unfolding sense of scale, it is one of Debussy’s most vividly pictorial works.
L117/10.ctx: Composed in 1909–10 as the tenth of the Book 1 préludes, drawing on the medieval legend of the drowned city of Ys, whose cathedral was said to reappear periodically from beneath the sea off the coast of Brittany.
facts: Inspired by a Breton legend of a cathedral that rises from the sea.
Built on massive, bell-like parallel chords.
One of the most pictorially vivid of Debussy’s twenty-four préludes.

L123/12.about: Titled ’Fireworks’, a dazzling, virtuosic depiction of a fireworks display, closing the second book of préludes with a shimmering explosion of colour that quotes a fragment of the French national anthem, ’La Marseillaise’, in its closing bars, as though heard drifting from a distant Bastille Day celebration.
L123/12.ctx: Composed in 1912–13 as the last of the twelve préludes of Book 2, written on the eve of the First World War, a period when Debussy’s health and personal finances were both increasingly precarious.
facts: Closes the second book of préludes with a quotation from ’La Marseillaise’.
Depicts a fireworks display, likely for the French national holiday, Bastille Day.
Among the most technically demanding of Debussy’s twenty-four préludes.

L110/1.about: Titled ’Reflections in the Water’, a shimmering evocation of light playing on the surface of water, built from rippling figuration and washes of harmony that blur conventional distinctions between melody and accompaniment.
L110/1.ctx: Composed in 1904–05 as the first piece of Images, Book 1, from a period when Debussy was consolidating the harmonic and pianistic innovations that would define his mature style, moving further from traditional tonal structure toward pure colour and atmosphere.
facts: Depicts light reflecting on moving water.
The first piece of Images, Book 1.
One of the most celebrated examples of musical Impressionism.

L113/6.about: A playful, syncopated parody closing Debussy’s suite Children’s Corner, mimicking the American cakewalk dance craze then fashionable in Paris, and slyly quoting and mocking the opening motif of Wagner’s Tristan und Isolde in its jazzy central section.
L113/6.ctx: Composed 1906–08 as the last of the six pieces of Children’s Corner, which Debussy dedicated ’to my dear little Chouchou, with her father’s tender apologies for what follows’ — addressed to his young daughter, though the suite’s technical demands make it unlikely a small child could actually play it.
facts: Mimics the American cakewalk dance, then fashionable in Paris.
Playfully quotes and mocks the opening of Wagner’s Tristan und Isolde.
The last of the six pieces of Children’s Corner, dedicated to Debussy’s young daughter.

L66/1.about: An early, flowing work whose gently undulating melodic lines gave the pair of arabesques their title, evoking the decorative, curving lines of Islamic ornamental art. Lighter and more conventionally tonal than Debussy’s mature style, it remains one of his most popular short pieces.
L66/1.ctx: Composed in his mid-to-late twenties, before the harmonic innovations of his fully mature style, the piece shows Debussy still working within a late-Romantic idiom indebted to composers like Massenet, even as his individual voice begins to emerge.
facts: One of Debussy’s earliest widely popular works.
Its title refers to the decorative, curving lines of Islamic ornamental art.
Written before the harmonic innovations of his fully mature style.

L106.about: Titled ’The Isle of Joy’, a brilliant, ecstatic single-movement showpiece said to have been inspired by Watteau’s painting L’Embarquement pour Cythère, depicting lovers departing for an island of pleasure. One of Debussy’s most technically demanding and exuberant piano works.
L106.ctx: Composed in 1903–04, during the period surrounding his opera Pelléas et Mélisande and his affair with Emma Bardac, who would later become his second wife — a personally turbulent time that coincided with some of his most sensuous, high-spirited music.
facts: Reportedly inspired by Watteau’s painting L’Embarquement pour Cythère.
Composed during the turbulent period of Debussy’s affair with his future second wife.
Among the most technically demanding of Debussy’s piano works.

L100/1.about: Titled ’Pagodas’, an evocation of Javanese gamelan music that Debussy had heard performed at the 1889 Paris Exposition Universelle, using pentatonic scales and layered, bell-like textures to suggest the sound world of Southeast Asian percussion orchestras.
L100/1.ctx: Composed in 1903 as the first piece of Estampes (’Prints’), a set of three pieces each evoking a different exotic locale; the gamelan music Debussy encountered at the 1889 Exposition left a lasting mark on his harmonic imagination, evident here and in several later works.
facts: Evokes Javanese gamelan music Debussy heard at the 1889 Paris Exposition.
The first piece of the set Estampes (’Prints’).
Uses pentatonic scales to suggest Southeast Asian percussion orchestras.

L95/3.about: A brilliant, relentlessly energetic moto perpetuo closing the suite Pour le piano, harking back, like the suite’s other two movements, to Baroque dance forms while filtering them through Debussy’s own harmonic language.
L95/3.ctx: Composed in 1901, part of a suite whose three movements — Prélude, Sarabande and this Toccata — pay homage to Baroque keyboard forms, reflecting a broader early-twentieth-century French interest in reviving and reinterpreting earlier national musical traditions.
facts: Closes the suite Pour le piano, which revisits Baroque dance forms.
One of Debussy’s most virtuosic and technically demanding pieces.
Part of an early-twentieth-century French revival of interest in Baroque forms.

L68.about: A gentle, wistfully melodic early piece that became unexpectedly popular decades after its composition, though Debussy himself later regarded it as a minor, hastily written work and was reportedly embarrassed by its commercial success.
L68.ctx: Composed in 1890 and published the same year, likely written quickly to meet a publisher’s commercial demand for an accessible salon piece, from a period before Debussy’s mature harmonic language had fully emerged.
facts: Debussy reportedly regarded it as a minor work despite its popularity.
Composed early in his career, before his mature style emerged.
Its gentle, songlike melody has made it one of his most popular early pieces.

L86.about: A hazy, sensuous orchestral tone poem inspired by a poem of Stéphane Mallarmé depicting a faun’s drowsy, half-remembered erotic reverie in the afternoon heat. Often considered the work that inaugurated musical Impressionism and, with it, the beginning of twentieth-century music, for its dissolution of clear harmonic direction, metre and thematic development in favour of pure atmosphere and colour.
L86.ctx: Composed in 1892–94, the piece grew out of Debussy’s long fascination with Mallarmé’s poetry and Symbolist aesthetics; the composer Pierre Boulez later called its flute opening the moment modern music began to ’wake’ from the constraints of the nineteenth century.
facts: Widely considered the founding work of musical Impressionism.
Inspired by a poem by Stéphane Mallarmé.
Pierre Boulez called its opening the moment modern music began.
